items.stem: Which is the largest storage of fresh water?
items.answer: Ice caps and glaciers
items.markingKey: Ice caps and glaciers. Antarctica alone holds about 60% of the world's fresh water.

items.stem: A student claims: "Groundwater is a renewable resource everywhere." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Fossil groundwater (e.g. the Nubian Sandstone Aquifer) recharges extremely slowly and is effectively non-renewable.
items.markingKey: Fossil groundwater (e.g. the Nubian Sandstone Aquifer) recharges extremely slowly and is effectively non-renewable. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: State two differences between a transfer and a transformation in the hydrological cycle.
items.answer: A transfer moves water without change of state (runoff, throughflow, advection); a transformation changes state (evaporation, condensation, freezing).
items.markingKey: A transfer moves water without change of state (runoff, throughflow, advection); a transformation changes state (evaporation, condensation, freezing). [1] per valid, explicit comparison up to [3].

items.stem:
Resource booklet, data extract on Himalayan glaciers and the Indus basin: "Glacier and snowmelt contribute about 40-60% of the Indus flow, supporting irrigation for over 200 million people."

Using evidence from the extract, analyse what it shows about glaciers as freshwater storages.
items.answer: Ice stores water in winter and releases it in summer; shrinking glaciers will reduce long-term flows.
items.markingKey: Evidence quoted from the extract with figures/units [1]; Ice stores water in winter and releases it in summer; shrinking glaciers will reduce long-term flows. [1] per valid linked point up to [3].

items.stem: With reference to the Amazon "flying rivers", explain how it illustrates the role of vegetation in the hydrological cycle.
items.answer: Forest transpiration recycles moisture that is carried west and south, supplying rainfall to farmland in southern Brazil and Argentina. Evapotranspiration is a major flow returning water to the atmosphere, so deforestation can reduce rainfall far away.
items.markingKey: Context (Forest transpiration recycles moisture that is carried west and south, supplying rainfall to farmland in southern Brazil and Argentina.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Evapotranspiration is a major flow returning water to the atmosphere, so deforestation can reduce rainfall far away. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the role of vegetation in the hydrological cycle.

items.stem: Using the case study and your own knowledge, evaluate the view that groundwater should be managed as a non-renewable resource.
items.answer: Groundwater should be managed according to recharge rate; fossil and slowly recharging aquifers should be treated as non-renewable.
items.markingKey: Strengths / supporting points: many aquifers recharge far slower than abstraction (Ogallala, North China Plain); fossil aquifers do not recharge. Limitations / counter-points: shallow aquifers in humid regions recharge quickly; managed aquifer recharge can replenish stores. Conclusion: Groundwater should be managed according to recharge rate; fossil and slowly recharging aquifers should be treated as non-renewable. [6]: award [1] for each valid, developed evaluative point (strength or limitation) up to [4], and up to [2] for a balanced, justified conclusion; at least one point must refer explicitly to the case study for full marks.

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "evapotranspiration".
items.answer: The combined loss of water to the atmosphere by evaporation from surfaces and transpiration from plants
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the combined loss of water to the atmosphere by evaporation from surfaces and transpiration from plants. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Distinguish between percolation and infiltration.
items.answer: Infiltration is water entering the soil from the surface; percolation is the deeper movement of water from the soil into underlying rock to become groundwater.
items.markingKey: Infiltration is water entering the soil from the surface; percolation is the deeper movement of water from the soil into underlying rock to become groundwater. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Evaluate the claim that human activity now has a greater influence on the hydrological cycle than natural processes in many drainage basins. [9]
items.answer: In heavily developed basins human influence is dominant locally, but natural climate drivers still control the global cycle.
items.markingKey: Indicative content - arguments supporting the statement: dams store huge volumes (Three Gorges); groundwater abstraction lowers water tables; urbanisation changes runoff. items.stem: Why does upwelling increase productivity?
items.answer: It brings nutrient-rich water to the sunlit surface
items.markingKey: It brings nutrient-rich water to the sunlit surface. Nitrate and phosphate are often limiting at the surface.

items.stem: Distinguish between El Niño and La Niña.
items.answer: In El Niño trade winds weaken, warm water spreads east and upwelling off Peru weakens; in La Niña trade winds strengthen, upwelling intensifies and the eastern Pacific is cooler than normal.
items.markingKey: In El Niño trade winds weaken, warm water spreads east and upwelling off Peru weakens; in La Niña trade winds strengthen, upwelling intensifies and the eastern Pacific is cooler than normal. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Lukas writes: "Ocean currents only move water near the surface." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Thermohaline circulation moves deep water throughout the ocean basins, taking about 1,000 years to complete a circuit.
items.markingKey: Thermohaline circulation moves deep water throughout the ocean basins, taking about 1,000 years to complete a circuit. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Briefly describe the weakening AMOC and explain what it reveals about thermohaline circulation as a potential tipping point.
items.answer: Studies suggest the AMOC is at its weakest in over 1,000 years, partly due to Greenland meltwater. Freshening of North Atlantic surface water reduces sinking and could cause abrupt regional climate change.
items.markingKey: Context (Studies suggest the AMOC is at its weakest in over 1,000 years, partly due to Greenland meltwater.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Freshening of North Atlantic surface water reduces sinking and could cause abrupt regional climate change. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to thermohaline circulation as a potential tipping point.

items.stem: Outline two effects of a strong El Niño on people and ecosystems.
items.answer: e.g. collapse of anchoveta catches in Peru; floods in Peru and Ecuador; droughts in Indonesia and Australia (forest fires in 1997-98); global coral bleaching.
items.markingKey: e.g. collapse of anchoveta catches in Peru; floods in Peru and Ecuador; droughts in Indonesia and Australia (forest fires in 1997-98); global coral bleaching.

items.stem: Give one strength and one limitation of the claim that changes in ocean circulation pose a greater threat to human societies than sea-level rise.
items.answer: Sea-level rise is the more certain threat, while circulation changes are a lower-probability but high-impact risk.
items.markingKey: For: AMOC collapse could cool Europe and disrupt monsoons. Against: sea-level rise is certain and already affecting coastal cities and islands. items.stem: Where does deep water form in the North Atlantic to drive thermohaline circulation?
options: At the equator
In the Mediterranean only
Off the coast of Peru
Near Greenland and the Labrador and Nordic Seas
items.answer: Near Greenland and the Labrador and Nordic Seas
items.markingKey: D. Cold, salty water sinks there.

items.stem:
Case study extract - the Peruvian anchoveta fishery and El Niño: Catches fell from about 12 million t in 1970 to under 2 million t in 1973 after the 1972-73 El Niño combined with overfishing.

Using the extract and your own knowledge, explain how this case illustrates the dependence of productivity on upwelling.
items.answer: Warm El Niño water suppressed upwelling of nutrients, cutting plankton and fish numbers, while heavy fishing removed the remaining stock.
items.markingKey: Warm El Niño water suppressed upwelling of nutrients, cutting plankton and fish numbers, while heavy fishing removed the remaining stock. items.answer: Weaker trade winds reduce upwelling; warm, nutrient-poor water lowers phytoplankton productivity; anchoveta move deeper or south or die, so catches fall.

About 30%
About 95%
About 10%
items.answer: About 70%

items.stem: Explain the difference between water withdrawal and water consumption.
items.answer: Withdrawal is water taken from a source (some returned, e.g. cooling water); consumption is water used and not returned to the source, e.g. lost by evapotranspiration from irrigated crops.
items.markingKey: Withdrawal is water taken from a source (some returned, e.g. cooling water); consumption is water used and not returned to the source, e.g. lost by evapotranspiration from irrigated crops. items.stem: With the help of a specific example, explain how climate change threatens water security.
items.answer: Changes in precipitation patterns, more intense droughts, faster evaporation, shrinking glaciers and snowpacks, and sea-level rise causing salinisation of coastal aquifers. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.)

items.answer: Singapore combines local catchments covering two-thirds of its land, imports from Johor, NEWater (up to ~40% of demand) and desalination (up to ~25%). Diversifying supply and recycling reduces dependence on imports and increases water security.

A situation where water is available but people lack the investment, infrastructure or money to access it
The average time a water molecule spends in a storage, e.g. about 9 days in the atmosphere and over 3,000 years in the oceans

items.stem: Briefly explain why the residence time of water in the atmosphere is short while in the oceans it is long.
items.answer: The atmosphere stores a tiny volume (about 13,000 km³) relative to the large flows of evaporation and precipitation (about 500,000 km³/yr), so turnover is fast (~9 days); the oceans store about 1.3 billion km³ so turnover takes thousands of years.

items.stem: With reference to the Peruvian anchoveta fishery and El Niño, explain in detail the causes and consequences involved in the dependence of productivity on upwelling. [7]
items.answer: Catches fell from about 12 million t in 1970 to under 2 million t in 1973 after the 1972-73 El Niño combined with overfishing. Warm El Niño water suppressed upwelling of nutrients, cutting plankton and fish numbers, while heavy fishing removed the remaining stock. A second, contrasting example should be developed in the same way.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "evapotranspiration"?

A situation where water resources are insufficient to meet demand, typically in arid regions
The combined loss of water to the atmosphere by evaporation from surfaces and transpiration from plants

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "thermohaline circulation"?

The average time a water molecule spends in a storage, e.g. about 9 days in the atmosphere and over 3,000 years in the oceans

items.stem: Explain how thermohaline circulation redistributes heat.
items.answer: Warm surface currents carry heat poleward (Gulf Stream); at high latitudes water cools, becomes saltier as sea ice forms, sinks and returns towards the equator at depth, so the system transports heat from the tropics to high latitudes.

items.stem: Explain the difference between blue water and green water.
items.answer: Green water is rainwater held in soil and used by crops (no abstraction); blue water is withdrawn from rivers, lakes or aquifers, often for irrigation, and competes with other uses.

items.stem: Explain the difference between economic water scarcity and physical water scarcity.
items.answer: Physical scarcity means there is not enough water to meet demand (e.g. the Middle East, Arizona); economic scarcity means water exists but people cannot access it due to lack of investment or money (e.g. much of sub-Saharan Africa).
